awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Tactile-enabled Robotic Quality Control Cell
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research Phase I project addresses significant challenges in manufacturing and agriculture by enhancing the capabilities of robotic automation with tactile sensing. Tactile-enabled robotic cells will allow robots to perform complex tasks such as gauge checking in machining and quality sorting of agricultural products. Often in a robotic pick-and-place operation, an object needs to be moved from an assembly line to a quality assurance (QA) step prior to packaging (for example). Combining this pick-and-place operation and QA step inherently saves time – creating a clear value proposition. By integrating advanced touch-based sensing technology into robotic grippers, this project promises substantial improvements in efficiency, accuracy, and safety in manufacturing quality control and agricultural sorting. Consequently, it supports national interests by strengthening U.S. competitiveness, reducing workplace injuries associated with repetitive manual tasks, and fostering job creation in advanced technical fields such as robotics and automation engineering.

The technical objective of this project involves developing a novel robotic handling system integrated with advanced tactile sensing capabilities. This project seeks to overcome the limitations of traditional robotic systems, which rely heavily on visual sensing and struggle to manage delicate or irregular objects. The innovation will enable robots to perform complex handling and quality assessment tasks through tactile feedback. Unlike vision systems, where the camera passively collects data from an object without interacting with it, touch-based systems require object interaction. The data received from the tactile sensors is highly dependent on the movements made by the gripper fingers. Thus, the handling unit and sensors must be designed together in order to extract haptic properties like object stiffness. A primary high-risk factor lies in creating robust tactile sensors capable of accurately measuring object interaction properties under challenging real-world conditions. Existing tactile sensors often lack durability, have limited resolution, slow framerate and cannot reliably operate in harsh industrial environments. Furthermore, this project proposes a unique design featuring a limited number of physical sensors and a method to create virtual “taxels” to greatly up-sample the resolution of the device. This technique seeks to significantly increase sensor resolution without increasing hardware complexity.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Robots are very good at moving quickly and repeating the same motion, but they are surprisingly poor at the kind of delicate, informed touch that people use without thinking — judging how firmly to hold a ripe piece of fruit, or feeling whether a machined part fits a gauge. Most robotic grippers are effectively numb: they can open and close, but they cannot feel what they are holding. This NSF Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project asked whether a low-cost robotic gripper could be given a useful sense of touch, and whether that touch information could be turned into decisions a robot can act on.

Sensate Robotics developed a tactile sensing fingertip, called the PolySkin sensor, together with the parallel-jaw gripper that carries it. Each fingertip is built from soft, rubber-like layers molded over a small circuit board. Tiny infrared lights shine into the soft material, and light detectors underneath watch how the light changes as the surface is pressed and deformed. From those changing light patterns the sensor estimates how hard it is being pressed and where on the fingertip the contact occurs. A second sensing mode passes a harmless electrical signal through the outer layer to measure an object's electrical impedance — a property that changes as fruit ripens and its internal structure softens — giving the gripper a way to gauge ripeness that a camera cannot see.

The work followed three tracks: building and testing the sensor, developing the software that interprets its signals, and designing the gripper itself.

On the sensor, the team built working prototypes and measured their performance against engineering targets. The sensors responded smoothly across a wide range of forces without losing sensitivity, repeated their readings consistently, and could distinguish contacts only a few millimeters apart — fine enough for the intended tasks. The team also compared nine combinations of rubber hardness and thickness and learned how each choice trades off force sensitivity against fine spatial detail, providing a clear recipe for tuning future sensors to specific jobs.

On the software, the team adapted a mathematical imaging technique — diffuse optical tomography, originally developed for medical imaging — to turn a handful of light measurements into a much higher-resolution picture of where and how hard the fingertip is being touched. A key discovery was that a simpler, faster version of the method works far better for touch sensing than the textbook approach: the improved method runs in about 31 milliseconds per frame, fast enough for a robot to use in real time, and reconstructs a touch image roughly 250 times more detailed than the raw sensor alone would provide.

On the gripper, the team completed the mechanical design of a compact, low-cost parallel-jaw gripper and built a working prototype. The design uses an inexpensive sliding-guide approach in place of the costlier precision bearings normally required, which also makes the gripper easier to seal against dust and water. Bench testing of the prototype's grip force and mechanical efficiency was completed: the grip force proved smooth, predictable, and repeatable in response to the motor’s command, and the low-cost sliding guide delivered enough of its theoretical force to meet the project’s efficiency target, retiring the principal mechanical risk of the new design.

The team also tested the gripper’s second sense — electrical impedance — on real produce. Using only its two fingertips, it reliably told over-ripe avocados from firm ones by their electrical signature, an early demonstration that it can judge internal ripeness a camera cannot see. Making this a calibrated, fruit-by-fruit measurement is a primary goal of the follow-on work.

Taken together, the Phase I results show that an affordable robotic gripper can be given practical, multi-sense touch — force, contact location, and a measure of internal quality — and that this information can be processed quickly enough for real use.

The broader impacts are economic and practical. Many manufacturing and food-handling tasks still depend on manual labor because today's robots cannot feel what they handle. A low-cost sensing gripper could help automate repetitive, injury-prone inspection and sorting work, strengthen U.S. manufacturing competitiveness, and reduce waste in fresh-produce supply chains through more consistent grading. During Phase I the company completed a structured customer-discovery program and identified two early markets — automated dimensional inspection of machined parts, and ripeness-based sorting of high-value produce such as avocados and strawberries — and began engaging prospective customers and an established robot-integration channel to move the technology toward commercial use.
